top_choice_rationale: P001 (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) is the strongest on originality, breadth, durability and maturity. Each laureate has a separable originating contribution: the tractable time-dependent pricing device, staggered contracts with the policy-rule framework, and the microfounded welfare-based framework for policy evaluation. The later literature on estimation, canonical models and central-bank adoption builds on these, and the citation can credit the originating ideas without claiming the framework has been validated by the post-2021 inflation. The costs are real: any trio excludes Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum and Smets, priority questions involving Fischer and Phelps are unresolved, and state-dependent pricing evidence limits Calvo pricing as a literal description. I still judge them smaller than the weight of B001's influence on how monetary policy is analysed. P002 is a close second because its credit boundary is cleaner and the work is mature. Its weaker cross-country identification and the neighbouring 2024 institutions prize count against it. P003 is a sound third: the selection model is directly tested on firm-level data and the attribution is a clean pair, but Melitz's contribution is concentrated in one paper, the empirical pioneers are outside the entry, and it follows the 2008 trade prize. I rank all three awards above no award because each is a mature, substantive achievement.
recusal_note: Disclosed, not adjudicated. I am at IIES and have long-standing co-authorship with John Hassler (chair) and Timo Boppart, the latter including the 2018 Myrdal Prize article. Other members' files refer to Torsten Persson (P002) as an IIES colleague. My research field of heterogeneous-agent macro is a successor literature to the framework in P001. My profile records no tie to Calvo, Taylor, Woodford, Helpman or Melitz.
